## Host classification

Host role is derived from `host.lineage` rank, not substring matching:

| Observed | Count | Role |
|---|---|---|
| Rodentia | 11,043 | `reservoir_rodent` |
| *Homo sapiens* | 2,091 | `spillover_host_human` |
| Eulipotyphla | 1,035 | `reservoir_shrew_mole` |
| Chiroptera | 83 | `reservoir_bat` |
| `isLabHost` true | 338 | `laboratory_host` |

`isLabHost`, `labHost` and `isVaccineStrain` are authoritative NCBI fields and are used directly;
lab-derived and vaccine records are excluded from the ML matrix.

**Host jumps.** Each record's host order is compared against its species' expected reservoir
order. 33 records are pathogenic viruses recovered outside their reservoir order — SEOV in
Chinese shrews and bats, ANDV-clade sequences in Brazilian bats. These are documented
host-sharing observations, not data errors, and are surfaced as
`host_jump_status = host_order_mismatch` and weighted in the risk score.

## Pathogenicity labels

`SPECIES_RISK` covers 38 species. Every entry carries its source URL. Species **absent** from the
table are labelled `unknown` — never silently "non-pathogenic".

CFR estimates genuinely conflict between sources, so the reported range is stored verbatim
alongside an ordinal band for modelling. Do not collapse them to a point estimate.

| Class | Species | CFR band |
|---|---|---|
| `pathogenic_hcps` | ANDV, SNV, CHOV, LANV, RIOMV, BAYV, BCCV | up to `high_gt_30pct` |
| `pathogenic_hfrs` | HTNV, DOBV, SEOV, PUUV | `low_lt_1pct` – `moderate_1_15pct` |
| `rare_or_opportunistic` | TULV | `low_lt_1pct` |
| `suspected` | THAIV, SANGV | `unknown` |
| `no_known_human_disease` | shrew-, mole- and bat-borne species | `none_known` |
| `unknown` | anything not curated | `unknown` |

HTNV is reported as both ~1% and 5–15% depending on source; both appear in `cfr_reported_range`.
ANDV is the only orthohantavirus with documented person-to-person transmission. TULV is held out
of `pathogenic_hfrs` deliberately — lumping its handful of mild case reports with HTNV/DOBV would
put 2,123 records into the same class as the viruses that actually drive HFRS mortality.

**Curation audit.** Curated reservoirs are checked against the modal observed host order on every
run. Six of the original 38 entries disagreed with the package's own host annotations at the order
level (asikkalaense, fugongense, lankaense, luxiense, sagercreekense, tigrayense) and were
corrected against the data. The audit runs every invocation so this class of error cannot silently
return.

"""Build the ML feature matrix and the scaling artifact.

    Two deliberate changes from the previous implementation:

    - Features are emitted RAW. The previous version z-scored every column across the
      whole dataset before writing, which leaks test-fold statistics into training. The
      per-column mean/std are written to ortho_feature_scaling.json instead, so scaling
      can be fitted inside the caller's cross-validation fold.
    - Feature selection is unsupervised (top-variance k-mers). The previous selector
      scored features as abs(between)/variance against label indices produced by sorting
      taxids alphabetically, which imposes an arbitrary ordinal scale on unordered
      categories.
    - group_id and year are included so downstream CV can split by species and by time.
      Random splits over this data overstate accuracy badly, because segments from the
      same outbreak are near-identical.
    """
    usable = [i for i in isolates if i.concatenated_protein_aa and not i.is_lab_derived
              and not i.is_vaccine_strain]

"""Build the ML feature matrix and the scaling artifact.

    Three deliberate changes from the previous implementation:

    - Features are emitted RAW. The previous version z-scored every column across the
      whole dataset before writing, which leaks test-fold statistics into training. The
      per-column mean/std are written to ortho_feature_scaling.json instead, so scaling
      can be fitted inside the caller's cross-validation fold.
    - Feature selection is unsupervised (top-variance k-mers). The previous selector
      scored features as abs(between)/variance against label indices produced by sorting
      taxids alphabetically, which imposes an arbitrary ordinal scale on unordered
      categories.
    - group_id and year are included so downstream CV can split by species and by time.
      Random splits over this data overstate accuracy badly, because segments from the
      same outbreak are near-identical.

    is_lab_derived is now FLAGGED, not filtered. An earlier version excluded every
    is_lab_derived isolate from this matrix, on the same "not a naturally occurring
    sample" reasoning --phylogenetics still uses. But NCBI's isLabHost field marks the
    immediate recorded host, not sequence provenance: of 164 is_lab_derived isolates, 21
    have host_taxid 9606 -- these are lab-acquired/occupational human infections in
    exactly the highest-CFR species (HTNV, ANDV, PUUV, DOBV) -- and most of the rest are
    samples from colony-maintained reservoir animals (Mus musculus, Rattus norvegicus,
    Apodemus agrarius), not attenuated or culture-adapted sequences. Blanket-filtering
    them discarded real positive evidence of human/reservoir infection for a
    pathogenicity-prediction task, exactly the risk this row's own citation warns about
    (https://microbiomejournal.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s40168-025-02059-0 --
    human-derived sequence similarity to reservoir sequences is itself the spillover-risk
    signal; excluding it removes the baseline). is_vaccine_strain isolates remain
    excluded: a vaccine strain is deliberately attenuated, so labelling its sequence with
    its parent species' wild-type pathogenicity class would inject a real, not
    hypothetical, false signal. --phylogenetics is unaffected by this: it keeps excluding
    both is_lab_derived and is_vaccine_strain, because a passage/attenuation history is a
    tree-topology risk (branch-length distortion) regardless of whether the sequence
    itself is informative for a similarity/classification feature.
    """
    usable = [i for i in isolates if i.concatenated_protein_aa and not i.is_vaccine_strain]

    isolates: Sequence[IsolateRecord],
    divergence_by_key: Dict[str, SegmentDivergenceProfile],
    cds_index: Dict[str, List[Tuple[str, str]]],

    """Extract the three named candidate groups and require full S+M+L CDS for each.

    The three groups -- human-affecting-or-likely, divergence candidates (already
    flagged 'requires_phylogenetic_confirmation' by the k-mer diagnostic), complete
    triplets -- are UNIONED, not intersected: each is independently a reason this
    isolate matters for the reassortment/pathogenicity goal. But a topology-incongruence
    test needs every isolate placed in all three segment trees, so 'CDS available for S,
    M and L' is a hard requirement on top of the union, not an optional nicety. Lab-
    derived and vaccine-strain isolates are excluded for the same reason they are
    excluded from the ML matrix: they are not naturally occurring samples.
    """
    exclusions: Counter = Counter()
    candidates: List[PhyloCandidate] = []

git commit -m "$(cat <<'EOF'
Flag lab-derived isolates in the ML matrix instead of filtering them

build_ml_tables previously excluded every is_lab_derived isolate, using the
same rationale --phylogenetics uses for excluding them from tree-building.
But NCBI's isLabHost field marks the immediate recorded host, not sequence
contamination: of 164 is_lab_derived isolates, 21 have host_taxid 9606 --
lab-acquired/occupational human infections concentrated in the highest-CFR
species (HTNV, ANDV, PUUV, DOBV) -- and most of the rest are samples from
colony-maintained reservoir animals, not culture-adapted sequences.
Blanket-filtering them discarded real positive evidence of human/reservoir
infection for a pathogenicity-prediction task; a study comparing
human-derived and reservoir Orthohantavirus sequences for zoonotic-risk
assessment found the human sequences are themselves the spillover-risk
baseline, not noise to remove
(https://microbiomejournal.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s40168-025-02059-0).

is_lab_derived isolates are now kept and exposed as an explicit
is_lab_derived column so a model can be trained/compared with or without
them. is_vaccine_strain isolates (2) remain excluded: deliberate
attenuation would inject a real label error, not a hypothetical one.

--phylogenetics is unaffected: it keeps excluding both is_lab_derived and
is_vaccine_strain, since passage/attenuation history is a tree-topology
risk (branch-length distortion) independent of whether a sequence is
informative as an ML feature. Verified: default pipeline counts unchanged
(15,991/39/9,852/223), --phylogenetics candidate selection unchanged
(1,464/17 split), ML feature matrix grows 7,498 -> 7,651 rows (+153
lab-derived isolates, 21 of them real human infections).

Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
EOF
)"

2075	    genuinely interesting observation (SEOV in Chinese shrews and bats, ANDV-clade

2092	    """Transparent additive priority score.

def species_risk_profile(species_name: str) -> Dict[str, Any]:
    """Look up curated risk metadata. Unlisted species are 'unknown', never 'safe'.

    Cached: this is a pure function over ~39 distinct species but is called once per row
    in every table builder, ~91k times per run. Callers must treat the returned dict as
    read-only.
    """
    entry = SPECIES_RISK.get(species_name)
    if entry is None:
        return {
            "virus_abbrev": "",
            "disease_syndrome": "unknown",
            "cfr_band": -1,
            "cfr_band_label": CFR_BAND_LABEL[-1],
            "cfr_reported_range": "",
            "reservoir_host": "",
            "endemic_region": "",
            "pathogenicity_class": "unknown",
            "risk_citation": "",
            "reservoir_order": "",
        }
    band = entry["cfr_band"]
    syndrome = entry["syndrome"]
    pathogenicity = SYNDROME_TO_PATHOGENICITY.get(syndrome, "unknown")
    return {
        "virus_abbrev": entry["abbrev"],
        "disease_syndrome": syndrome,
        "cfr_band": band,
        "cfr_band_label": CFR_BAND_LABEL.get(band, CFR_BAND_LABEL[-1]),
        "cfr_reported_range": entry["cfr_reported"],
        "reservoir_host": entry["reservoir"],
        "endemic_region": entry["region"],
        "pathogenicity_class": pathogenicity,
        "risk_citation": entry["citation"],
        "reservoir_order": RESERVOIR_GENUS_ORDER.get(entry["reservoir"].split()[0], ""),
    }


def host_jump_status(observed_order: str, reservoir_order: str) -> str:
    """Compare the sampled host's order against the species' expected reservoir order.

    A pathogenic rodent-borne virus recovered from a shrew or bat is a documented and
    genuinely interesting observation (SEOV in Chinese shrews and bats, ANDV-clade
    sequences in Brazilian bats both appear in this package), not a data error.
    """
    if not observed_order or not reservoir_order:
        return "unknown"
    if observed_order == reservoir_order:
        return "expected_reservoir_order"
    if observed_order == "Primates":
        return "human_or_primate_spillover"
    return "host_order_mismatch"


def surveillance_priority(
    isolate: IsolateRecord,
    risk: Dict[str, Any],
    profile: Optional[SegmentDivergenceProfile],
) -> Dict[str, Any]:
    """Transparent additive priority score.

    Every term is emitted as its own column so the total can be audited, disagreed with
    or re-weighted downstream. This is a triage aid for surveillance, not a validated
    epidemiological risk model.

    Note: no term is derived from the k-mer segment-divergence diagnostics. An earlier
    version weighted them as reassortment evidence; that classifier failed validation
    against the literature (see compute_segment_divergence) and feeding it into a risk
    score would have propagated an artefact of sample size into a ranking meant to guide
    surveillance. Only taxonomic_incongruence -- a metadata fact -- contributes.
    """
    weights = SURVEILLANCE_WEIGHTS
    cfr_term = weights["cfr_by_band"].get(int(risk["cfr_band"]), 0.5)
    spillover_term = weights["human_spillover"] if isolate.host_role == "spillover_host_human" else 0.0
    incongruence_term = weights["taxonomic_incongruence"] if isolate.taxonomic_incongruence else 0.0
    jump_term = weights["host_jump"] if host_jump_status(
        isolate.host_order, risk["reservoir_order"]) == "host_order_mismatch" else 0.0
    completeness_term = weights["complete_triplet"] if isolate.has_complete_triplet else 0.0
    nss_term = weights["nss_orf"] if isolate.has_nss_orf else 0.0
    total = (cfr_term + spillover_term + incongruence_term + jump_term
             + completeness_term + nss_term)
    return {
        "priority_cfr_term": cfr_term,
        "priority_human_spillover_term": spillover_term,
        "priority_taxonomic_incongruence_term": incongruence_term,
        "priority_host_jump_term": jump_term,
        "priority_triplet_term": completeness_term,
        "priority_nss_term": nss_term,
        "surveillance_priority_score": round(total, 3),
    }


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Rigorous phylogenetic reassortment analysis -- opt-in via --phylogenetics
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
#
# Everything above (assign_kmer_clusters, compute_segment_divergence) is alignment-free
# and deliberately NOT a reassortment call -- see compute_segment_divergence's docstring
# for the validation failure that got that classifier withdrawn. This section is the
# real thing it pointed to: per-segment CDS-nucleotide alignments (MAFFT) and
# maximum-likelihood trees with ultrafast bootstrap support (IQ-TREE), compared for
# topological incongruence between S, M and L.
#
# It only runs when --phylogenetics is passed, requires mafft and iqtree on PATH (or
# --mafft-bin/--iqtree-bin), and Biopython + dendropy (imported lazily below so a
# default run never needs them). It only ever touches the three named candidate groups
# -- human-affecting-or-likely, divergence candidates, complete triplets -- and every
# candidate isolate is reported exactly once in the output table, tagged with why it was
# selected and, if analysis didn't happen, why not. Nothing is silently dropped.
#
# Setup:
#   conda create -n hanta_phylo -c bioconda -c conda-forge mafft iqtree biopython dendropy
#   conda activate hanta_phylo   # or pass --mafft-bin / --iqtree-bin with full paths

HUMAN_AFFECTING_CLASSES = {"pathogenic_hcps", "pathogenic_hfrs", "rare_or_opportunistic", "suspected"}

# CDS sequences shorter than this cannot be meaningfully aligned or placed in a tree --
# a floor against corrupt/truncated annotations, not a completeness filter.
MIN_CDS_LENGTH = 100

# Rank-separation thresholds for classify_reassortment_call. sl_rank_separation asks
# "do the S and L trees still agree on this isolate's neighbourhood" (should be LOW --
# S and L cosegregate per PMC6153690); m_rank_offset asks "is the M tree's answer
# different from S/L's" (should be HIGH for a genuine M-segment reassortant). Neither
# threshold is fitted to this data -- they mark the qualitative pattern the literature
# describes, and every candidate above them still has to clear the bootstrap gate below.
M_OFFSET_HIGH = 0.5
SL_SEPARATION_LOW = 0.35


def is_human_affecting_or_likely(pathogenicity_class: str, host_role: str) -> bool:
    """Curated pathogenic/suspected species, OR a species not yet curated but observed
    directly in a human host in this package -- the 'likely to affect humans' half of
    the brief that a static curated table alone cannot express.
    """
    if pathogenicity_class in HUMAN_AFFECTING_CLASSES:
        return True
    return pathogenicity_class == "unknown" and host_role == "spillover_host_human"

content.text:
Approach this as the design lead at a small studio known for their versatility, giving every client a visual identity pitched at the treatment the task actually calls for. Make deliberate choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this subject, and avoid templated designs.

## Read the request first

Calibrate treatment, not whether to design. A doc deserves the same craft as a landing page — what changes is the treatment that craft is delivered in.

Many requests call for a more utilitarian treatment: a plan, a memo, a demo. Make it polished: include real typographic hierarchy, considered spacing, and a proper palette, but avoid over-designing. Most pages do not need a flashy, gigantic hero. Keep flourishes tasteful and limited.

Some requests call for an editorial treatment: a landing page, a game, an app or tool they'll keep or share.

When unsure: a well-composed page is never the wrong answer; an over-designed visual identity sometimes is.

Fundamentals below apply to everything. The editorial process after that runs only when the read above says so.

## Fundamentals for every artifact

**Honor what's already there** Look for an existing design system first — CLAUDE.md, a tokens or theme file, existing component styles. When one exists, apply it; everything below fills gaps and never overrides. Precedence is always: the user's own words, then the project's existing system, then your choices.

**Ground it in the subject.** If the subject isn't already clear, pin it: one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job. The subject's own world — its materials, instruments, vernacular — is where distinctive choices come from. Build with real content throughout, never lorem.

**Pair typefaces** Typography carries the page even when the page isn't about typography. The Artifact CSP blocks font CDNs, so don't link a webfont URL and risk a silent fallback. Instead inline the face as a @font-face data URI. Keep running text near 65 characters wide; set a type scale and stay on it; give headings `text-wrap: balance`, body text room to breathe, and uppercase labels a touch of letter-spacing.

**Choose neutrals, don't default to them.** A pure mid-grey reads as unconsidered; a grey with a slight hue bias toward the page's accent reads as chosen. Pure white and near-black are fine grounds when they suit the subject — the point is that the neutral was picked, not inherited.

**Design both themes.** The page renders in the viewer's theme: `prefers-color-scheme` carries the OS preference, and the viewer's toggle stamps `data-theme="dark"` / `data-theme="light"` on the root element, which must override the media query in both directions. The robust pattern is token-level: define the palette as custom properties on `:root`, redefine only the tokens under `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` — style components through the tokens, never directly inside the media query — then redefine them again under `:root[data-theme="dark"]` and `:root[data-theme="light"]`. Give the second theme the same care as the first — don't naively invert; keep contrast legible and the accent working on both grounds. A design that deliberately commits to one visual world (a neon arcade screen, a letterpress invitation) may stay single-theme — make it a choice, not an omission.

**Let layout do the spacing.** Lay out sibling groups with flex or grid and `gap`, not per-element margins that silently collapse or double. Wide content — tables, code, diagrams — gets `overflow-x: auto` on its own container so the page body never scrolls sideways. Reach for `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` wherever digits line up in columns.

**Avoid AI-generated design** AI-generated design currently clusters around a few looks: warm cream (#F4F1EA) with a serif display and terracotta accent; near-black with a lone acid-green or vermilion pop; broadsheet hairline rules with dense columns; a purple-to-blue gradient hero on white; Inter or Space Grotesk as the "safe" face; emoji as section markers; everything centered; `rounded-lg` everywhere; accent bar/rail on rounded cards. Where the user pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly — their words always win, including when they ask for one of these looks. Where nothing is specified, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults.

**Build cleanly** Be cognizant of overlapping elements, cascade collisions, silent font fallbacks; visual bugs hide in the gap between source and output. Close every non-void element, double-quote attributes, give keyboard focus a visible state, respect `prefers-reduced-motion`. For generative or decorative graphics, reach for Canvas or WebGL rather than hand-authoring long SVG path data.

**CSS rules** When writing the CSS, watch your selector specificities. It is easy to generate classes that cancel each other out — a type-based selector like `.section` fighting an element-based one like `.cta` over padding and margins between sections. Structure the cascade so it doesn't silently undo your spacing.

**Writing the copy** Words are design material, not decoration. Write from the user's side of the screen — name things by what people recognize, not how the system is built (a person manages *notifications*, not *webhook config*). Active voice; a control says exactly what happens ("Publish", then a toast that says "Published"). Errors explain what went wrong and how to fix it — no apologies, no vagueness. Specific beats clever.

**Structure is information** Structural devices, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, should encode something true about the content, not decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence - like a real process or a typed timeline where order carries information the reader needs. Question if choices like numbered markers actually make sense before incorporating them.

**When it's a UI, not a document** A dashboard or tool is scanned and operated, not read top-to-bottom, so the craft shifts from typography to information design. Surface the summary before the detail; encode state in form as well as number — a pill, a chip, a severity stripe — so what needs attention reads at a glance. Semantic color (good / warning / critical) is separate from the accent hue and doesn't count as your accent. Give sparklines and charts the same care as type: an area fill, a faint grid, an emphasized endpoint. What's interactive should look interactive.



## Process

Before writing code, sketch a short design plan — a compact token system with color, type, and layout:
- **Color**: describe the palette as 4–6 named hex values.
- **Type**: typefaces for 2+ roles — a characterful display face used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed.
- **Layout**: a layout concept in one or two sentences.

Then build, following the plan and deriving every color and type decision from it.

## When the request is editorial

The stance shifts: the client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view. Make opinionated calls, and take one real aesthetic risk where it serves the work.

Review the design plan against the subject before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page, revise that part, and note what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the plan's uniqueness do you write the code, following the revised plan exactly.

**Principles** 

- The hero is a thesis: open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world — headline, image, live demo, interactive moment. 
- Typography carries the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, not the same families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content. 
- Leverage motion deliberately. Think about where and if animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, a scroll-triggered reveal, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. An orchestrated moment usually lands harder than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation contributes to the feeling that the design is AI-generated. 
- Match complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.
- Spend your boldness in one place; keep everything around it quiet. If the accent fights the ground, shift it toward analogous or drop saturation rather than replacing it.

The Orthohantavirus Pipeline

What each branch is trying to do, how it actually does it, and — since you asked specifically — exactly how "how dangerous is this virus" gets turned into a number today.

Repo arman-daliri/Orthohantavirus Branches covered main · check/reassortment · ml-lab-strain-flagging Status all three pushed to GitHub

Three branches, one growing pipeline. main turns a raw NCBI download into clean, labelled, analysis-ready tables — no phylogenetics, no ML training, just very carefully verified bookkeeping. check/reassortment adds the first branch's missing piece: real alignments and trees to test whether a virus's three genome segments have been genetically reshuffled. ml-lab-strain-flagging fixes a data-inclusion bug in the machine-learning table that was quietly throwing away some of the most informative rows. What "reassortment" means for a three-piece genome

Aim. A published comparison of human-derived and reservoir-derived Orthohantavirus sequences found that human-derived sequences are the actual baseline for judging spillover risk — not noise to be cleaned out. This branch checks that claim against the pipeline and fixes what it found.

main excluded every isolate NCBI marks isLabHost from both the phylogenetics candidate pool and the ML feature matrix, using the same justification for both: "not a naturally occurring sample." IV.

What's still missing

The honest part

The stated end goal — train on pathogenic, complete-triplet, reassortment-informed isolates and produce a confidence score for a brand-new, never-seen sequence — is not built yet. Everything in Sections I–III is the (now solid) data preparation for that model: clean labels, real phylogenetic diagnostics, and a training table that no longer throws away good rows. But there is no sklearn, no train/test split, no similarity search, and no scored prediction anywhere in the code today. surveillance_priority_score only ranks isolates of species we've already curated by hand — it cannot say anything about a species that isn't in that table yet, which is exactly the case a novel-pathogen predictor needs to handle.

The pieces that exist and are ready to be built on: a leakage-safe raw feature matrix with proper CV grouping, curated pathogenicity labels with citations, real per-segment phylogenetic distances, and (now) an honestly-populated lab/wild-type flag instead of a silently shrunk training set. The next real step is choosing a reference set (curated pathogenic + complete-triplet + phylogenetically-confirmed isolates), a similarity or classification method, and a validation strategy that respects the species/time grouping already built into the feature table — none of which has been written yet.

After the full run, an automated review found that the opt-in phylogenetics stage was wired in a way that could cost you the entire pipeline's output if it failed — e.g. if MAFFT or IQ-TREE weren't installed, every core table (accessions, isolates, species, risk, ML matrix) would go unwritten too, because the phylogenetics step ran before them and had no error boundary of its own. Both issues are fixed: the opt-in stage now runs strictly after every core table is safely on disk, and is wrapped so its own failure can only ever cost you the reassortment table, never the rest of the run.

III.

ml-lab-strain-flagging — recovering training signal we were throwing away

Aim. A published comparison of human-derived and reservoir-derived Orthohantavirus sequences found that human-derived sequences are the actual baseline for judging spillover risk — not noise to be cleaned out. This branch checks that claim against the pipeline and fixes what it found.

One flag, two very different meanings

main excluded every isolate NCBI marks isLabHost from both the phylogenetics candidate pool and the ML feature matrix, using the same justification for both: "not a naturally occurring sample." But isLabHost records the immediate recorded host, not sequence contamination. Of 164 is_lab_derived isolates:

  • 21 have host_taxid 9606 — real human infections, almost certainly lab-acquired/occupational exposure, concentrated in exactly the species where "does this virus hurt humans" matters most: Hantaan (16 records), Andes (3), Puumala (1), Dobrava (1).
  • Most of the rest are samples from colony-maintained reservoir animals (lab mice, lab rats, lab-housed striped field mice) — not culture-adapted or attenuated sequences.
  • Only 2 isolates are true vaccine strains — deliberately attenuated, a genuinely different case.

Throwing all 164 away for a pathogenicity-prediction task discarded exactly the kind of positive evidence — "this exact virus is capable of infecting and harming a human" — that a model trying to predict human risk needs most.

The fix: flag, don't filter

Phylogenetics is untouched — building a tree still excludes lab-derived and vaccine isolates, because passage history is a genuine branch-length distortion risk regardless of whether the sequence is otherwise informative. The ML matrix now keeps is_lab_derived isolates and exposes the flag as its own column, so a model can be trained and compared with or without them instead of losing the isolates outright. Vaccine strains stay excluded from the ML matrix too — attenuation is a real, not hypothetical, source of label error.

IV.

What's still missing

The honest part

The stated end goal — train on pathogenic, complete-triplet, reassortment-informed isolates and produce a confidence score for a brand-new, never-seen sequence — is not built yet. Everything in Sections I–III is the (now solid) data preparation for that model: clean labels, real phylogenetic diagnostics, and a training table that no longer throws away good rows. But there is no sklearn, no train/test split, no similarity search, and no scored prediction anywhere in the code today. surveillance_priority_score only ranks isolates of species we've already curated by hand — it cannot say anything about a species that isn't in that table yet, which is exactly the case a novel-pathogen predictor needs to handle.

The pieces that exist and are ready to be built on: a leakage-safe raw feature matrix with proper CV grouping, curated pathogenicity labels with citations, real per-segment phylogenetic distances, and (now) an honestly-populated lab/wild-type flag instead of a silently shrunk training set. The next real step is choosing a reference set (curated pathogenic + complete-triplet + phylogenetically-confirmed isolates), a similarity or classification method, and a validation strategy that respects the species/time grouping already built into the feature table — none of which has been written yet.

- **I. `main`** — the data foundation: taxonomy resolution, isolate reconstruction, host classification, pathogenicity labels, and a full walkthrough of `surveillance_priority_score` (the actual formula, the weight table, and two fully worked numeric examples — a human HTNV case scoring 5.5, a routine wild TULV case scoring 1.0) — plus a callout being explicit that this score is a hand-weighted heuristic over species we've already curated, not a trained predictor.

- **III. `ml-lab-strain-flagging`** — the lab-strain bug, why it mattered (21 real human infections were being thrown away), and the fix.
- **IV. What's still missing** — an honest statement that the actual novel-virus prediction model (the real end goal) hasn't been built yet — only its data foundation has.
